item.title: Collecting reference images with PureRef
item.content:
PureRef keeps your reference images together on one board, so you don't have to bring them into Photoshop and lay out a reference board by hand. In this part you'll download PureRef, collect images of your subject in a folder, open them as a board that floats above the software you're working in, save the board to come back to, and export it as a single image you can hand in. PureRef is free for personal use and runs on Windows, macOS and Linux. The video uses PureRef 2.0.1 on a Mac, so newer versions and the download page may look a little different.

Get PureRef

  1. Download PureRef. 0:08 Go to pureref.com and click Download. 0:19 Choose Personal, then your operating system.

  2. Choose an amount and install it. 0:28 PureRef asks you to pay what you like to support it. You can donate another time: choose $0, so the total reads Free, then click Download and install PureRef.

  3. Open PureRef. 0:44 A new board is empty: you can drag and drop images onto it, or click Browse to pick them from a folder.

Collect your images

  1. Search for images of your subject. 1:04 The video's example is a project on castles: what castles and their stonework looked like in a particular period, such as the medieval, and what a castle looks like at night. A web image search finds dozens to help you.

  2. Save them in a folder of references. 1:42 Drag each image you want from the browser into a folder on your computer. These images are only for you to look at, to give you ideas of what to make; they don't go into your finished work.

Make a reference board

  1. Bring in the images. 2:03 In PureRef, click Browse, go to your folder of references, select the images and click Open. PureRef brings them all in at once.

  2. Zoom out to see them all. 2:19 The images can be too big to see together. Press Cmd+- to zoom out, and you'll see them all packed together in a group.

  3. Look closer. 2:35 Double-click any image to see it at full size. 2:40 Resize the window to suit your screen.

  4. Keep the board on top. 2:44 Click the pin button at the top left of the window. Always on top keeps the board above all your other software; Always on top of… keeps it above particular software. 2:57 Move the board to a part of the screen you're not using, and it floats there, in view, while you work in something else.

    On a Mac, Always on top of… needs accessibility access, which you give PureRef in System Settings → Privacy & Security. The video doesn't, so it uses Always on top.

Save and share the board

  1. Save the board. 3:12 Choose File → Save, give the board a name (the video's is references-castle), choose where to keep it (the video uses the folder of references) and click Save. PureRef saves it as a .pur file, a PureRef scene.

  2. Export it as one image. 3:31 Choose File → Export → Scene. In Export scene, use the folder button to choose where to save the PNG, check its width and height, choose whether to include the background and borders, and click Export. 3:45 The PNG has all your images together, laid out as they are on the board: 3:58 a still image you can hand in when an assignment asks for your reference images.

  3. Come back to the board. 4:14 To use the board interactively again, double-click its .pur file to open it in PureRef, and double-click images to see them full size. 4:25 Drag images to space them out and arrange them however you like: there are no pixels or layers to worry about, as there would be in Photoshop.

That's the whole workflow: a folder of images, a board that stays in view while you work in other software, a .pur file to come back to, and a PNG to hand in when an assignment asks for your references.

Transcript

From speech to text.

0:00 I wanted to mention a tool that I like to use for my references whenever I'm working on a project. This one's called PureRef. So P-U-R-E-R-E-F dot com. And this is a really simple lightweight tool. It's free for personal use, cross operating system. But if we go to download here, we can go to personal and click on your operating system. And I'll just donate another time. So for the purposes of this we'll just say zero dollars and then click download and we'll go ahead and install this. So I already have this installed so I'm going to go ahead and open PureRef and what it is is essentially a way to interactively manage reference images so you don't have to manually bring things into something like Photoshop and create a large reference board manually. I'll just show you what it does to better explain.

1:04 So let's say I've done a bunch of work, you know, researching images of castles or something like that. Maybe I'm working on a project where I have to build something like this. I don't really know what they look like or what stonework used to look like from different time periods. So if I have a particular time period, let's say sometime in medieval time periods, I could look for that. But I can find dozens of images to help me. Let's say I want to see what it looks like at nighttime. Just as a reference for myself, I can grab this and drop this in a folder of references. So this is a folder on my computer where I'm dropping images into.

1:51 Again, I'm not using these in the final output of my project. These are just things that I can look at to give me an idea of what to create. So in PureRef, we can go ahead and browse to that folder. And then I'm going to select my reference images and click open. And what it does is imports dynamically all of those images. So if I scroll down, you can see they're kind of here. They're a little bit hard to see. So if I was to press Command-Minus, I can zoom out and effectively see all of them imported in a group like this.

2:35 I can also just double-click on any of them to make them full-size. I can resize the reference window here. And then the reference window allows me to pin it on top of particular software. But I can pin it on top of any of my other software. So for instance if I need to have this visible while I'm working on something else I can just kind of move it over to an area of the screen I'm not really using and just have that float there. I can save this out and I'll just call this references castle and I'll save that there. This saves it as a .pur file format. The other thing I can do is export this. So I can export all of them as a scene and I'm going to go ahead and create that in that same location. Okay, so just to show you what that does, I can basically have a PNG image of all of them

3:52 in the same area. And you know, this is something you could do with Photoshop or Illustrator. But what I like about it is if I want to use it as a static image, I can do that. So if I needed to submit all of my reference images, for instance, for an assignment requirement, I can do that here. Or if I just want to be able to use this interactively, when I double click, it will then kind of bring those reference images full screen for me. I can also rearrange them here within PureRef and kind of space them out anywhere I want.

4:33 So if I want to organize them, I can do that. And we're not really dealing with the overhead of worrying about pixels and layers and things like that. So that's the advantage of using a tool like PureRef. I definitely recommend it. It might speed up your workflow a little bit more when trying to get references together. Otherwise, yeah, give it a try and see if it fits with your workflow.
